```{julia}
#| output: false
using Plots
using Measures
using LaTeXStrings
using Roots

plot_font = "Palatino Roman"
default(
    fontfamily=plot_font,
    linewidth=3,
    framestyle=:box,
    label=nothing,
    grid=false,
    guidefontsize=18,
    legendfontsize=16,
    tickfontsize=16,
    titlefontsize=20,
    bottom_margin=10mm,
    left_margin=5mm
)

# Okabe-Ito palette: distinguishable under all common types of colour
# blindness. Red/green is the usual confusion pair, so eutrophication and
# recovery are coded vermillion vs blue, never red vs green -- and every
# pair is given a different line style as well, so the figures still read
# in greyscale.
cb_orange = "#E69F00"
cb_green = "#009E73"
cb_yellow = "#F0E442"
cb_blue = "#0072B2"
cb_vermillion = "#D55E00"
cb_purple = "#CC79A7"
```

```{julia}
#| output: false

# --- The shallow lake model, carried over from Lecture 05 -------------------
#
#   P_{t+1} = P_t + L - s*P_t + R(P_t),   R(P) = r * P^q / (m^q + P^q)
#
s = 0.6     # outflow + permanent burial               [1/yr]
r = 20.0    # maximum sediment release rate            [μg/(L⋅yr)]
m = 30.0    # P concentration at half-maximum release  [μg/L]
q = 8       # steepness of the sediment release        [-]

recycling_fraction(P, q) = (P / m)^q / (1 + (P / m)^q);
lake_P_release(P, q) = r * recycling_fraction(P, q);
lake_P_loss(P) = s * P;
lake_P_change(P, L, q) = L - lake_P_loss(P) + lake_P_release(P, q);

# Slope of the recycling curve, and the feedback gain (amplifying - dampening).
release_slope(P, q) = r * q * (P / m)^q / (P * (1 + (P / m)^q)^2);
feedback_gain(P, q) = release_slope(P, q) - s;

# The equilibrium condition, solved for L rather than P: L appears linearly,
# so sweeping P gives the whole curve including the unstable branch.
loading_for_P(P, q) = lake_P_loss(P) - lake_P_release(P, q);

# Both thresholds sit where the gain is zero.
eutrophic_P(q) = Roots.find_zero(P -> feedback_gain(P, q), (0.1, m));
recovery_P(q) = Roots.find_zero(P -> feedback_gain(P, q), (m, 80.0));
eutrophication_threshold(q) = loading_for_P(eutrophic_P(q), q);
recovery_threshold(q) = loading_for_P(recovery_P(q), q);

# Base-case equilibrium curve, split into stable and unstable branches.
Pb = 0.01:0.02:60.0
L_eq = loading_for_P.(Pb, q)
is_stable = feedback_gain.(Pb, q) .< 0
L_st = [st ? Lv : NaN for (Lv, st) in zip(L_eq, is_stable)]
L_un = [st ? NaN : Lv for (Lv, st) in zip(L_eq, is_stable)]
```

# What We Don't Know About $q$

## Which Parameter Do You Trust?

| | how you'd get it |
|:---|:---|
| $s$ | outflow gauging, sediment cores |
| $r$ | sediment incubations |
| $m$ | P--chlorophyll relationships |
| $q$ | **the shape of a switch nobody has watched flip** |

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
You only get calibration data on the transition **after** the lake has already tipped.

And $q$ decides whether the phenomenon exists at all: below $q \approx 3.6$ there is no second equilibrium at all, and no hysteresis.
:::

## Eutrophication and Recovery Bands

```{julia}
#| label: fig-q-bands
#| fig-cap: "Eutrophication and recovery thresholds across the plausible range of q, over the base-case equilibrium curve."
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true

q_vals = 4:0.25:20
Lc_all = eutrophication_threshold.(q_vals)
Lr_all = recovery_threshold.(q_vals)

p_band = plot(xlims=(0, 20), ylims=(0, 60), legend=:bottomright,
    xlabel="External loading L  [μg/(L⋅yr)]", ylabel="Equilibrium P  [μg/L]")

# Bands first, so the curves draw on top of them.
plot!(p_band, [minimum(Lr_all), maximum(Lr_all)], [0, 0], fillrange=[60, 60],
    color=cb_blue, alpha=0.22, linewidth=0, label="recovery, q = 4–20")
plot!(p_band, [minimum(Lc_all), maximum(Lc_all)], [0, 0], fillrange=[60, 60],
    color=cb_vermillion, alpha=0.22, linewidth=0, label="eutrophication, q = 4–20")

plot!(p_band, loading_for_P.(Pb, 4), Pb, color=:grey, alpha=0.5, linewidth=2, label=nothing)
plot!(p_band, loading_for_P.(Pb, 20), Pb, color=:grey, alpha=0.5, linewidth=2, label=nothing)
plot!(p_band, L_st, Pb, color=:black, linewidth=5, label="q = 8")
plot!(p_band, L_un, Pb, color=:black, linewidth=3, linestyle=:dash, label=nothing)

annotate!(p_band, (maximum(Lr_all) + minimum(Lc_all)) / 2, 54,
    text("no\noverlap", 14, :center))
plot!(p_band, size=(1150, 510), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm, bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)
```

## What Survives the Uncertainty

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=45%}
| $q$ | eutrophication | recovery |
|---:|---:|---:|
| $4$ | $8.7$ | $7.9$ |
| $6$ | $10.5$ | $6.6$ |
| $8$ | $11.7$ | $5.3$ |
| $12$ | $13.1$ | $3.6$ |
| $20$ | $14.6$ | $1.9$ |

Eutrophication moves $\times 1.7$.
Recovery moves $\times 4.3$.
The window moves $\times 16$.
:::
::: {.column width=55%}
**You can estimate roughly where you will break the lake. You cannot estimate what it will cost to fix it.**

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
But the two bands **do not overlap**.

So the *ordering* is robust even though every number is not: recovery is always harder than eutrophication. That conclusion you can defend; the budget figure you cannot.
:::
:::
::::
